transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to JPMorgan Chase's Third Quarter 26 Earnings Call. This call is being recorded. Information concerning forward-looking statements and non-GAAP financial measures included in this presentation can be found in JPMorgan Chase's earnings press release and investor presentation posted on the Investor Relations website. Please stand by. At this time, I would like to turn the call over to JPMorgan Chase's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, James Dimon, and Chief Financial Officer, Jeremy Barnum. Mr. Barnum, please go ahead.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Thank you very much, and good morning, everyone. The firm delivered net income of $15.3 billion, EPS of $5.57, and an ROTCE of 20%. These results included $658 million of net investment securities losses in Corporate. Revenue of $50.9 billion was up 8% year on year. Excluding the net investment securities losses, revenue was up 9% year on year, largely driven by markets revenue, higher deposit balances, and higher asset management fees in AWM. Expenses of $27.3 billion were up 12% year on year, largely driven by higher volume- and revenue-related expense, as well as front-office hiring and wage inflation. Credit costs were $2.7 billion, with net charge-offs of $2.2 billion and a net reserve build of $539 million. In terms of the balance sheet, we ended the quarter with a standardized CET1 ratio of 13.9%, down 30 basis points versus the prior quarter, as net income was more than offset by OCI losses, higher RWA, and capital distributions. You will note that we have updated the categories on the RWA walk to make it a bit more useful. This quarter's standardized RWA increase of about $52 billion was predominantly driven by an increase in lending across Banking, Markets, and AWM, as well as the impact of higher energy prices and increased market volatility. Now moving to our businesses. CCB reported net income of $5.7 billion. Revenue of $21.2 billion was up 9% year on year, predominantly driven by higher balances and yield at Card, asset management fees, deposit balances, and auto lease income. A few points to highlight: debit and credit spend grew 10% year on year, with continued momentum across spending categories, including gas and travel, supported by consumer demand. Deposit growth of 4% year on year was stronger this quarter as we continued to grow our customer base across Consumer and Business Banking, and we retained our number one position in retail deposit share based on FDIC data. Client investment assets crossed $1.4 trillion, up 15% year on year, driven by market performance and strong flows. Next, the CIB reported net income of $8.2 billion. Revenue of $22.7 billion was up 14% year on year on strong performance across the businesses. IB fees were up 14% year on year, reflecting strong performance across products, notably in advisory. While our outlook remains constructive, supported by ongoing client engagement, evolving market conditions have recently slowed activity a bit, so we will have to see how the quarter develops. In Markets, fixed income was down 4% year on year, with lower revenues in commodities, rates, and credit largely offset by higher client flows in currencies and emerging markets. Equities was up 49% year on year, with continued outperformance across the franchise, notably in prime and derivatives. Turning to Asset and Wealth Management. AWM reported net income of $1.8 billion, with a pretax margin of 36%. Revenue of $6.9 billion was up 14% year on year, predominantly driven by growth in management fees on higher average market levels, strong net inflows, as well as higher loan balances. Long-term net inflows were $51 billion, largely driven by continued strength in fixed income. AUM of $5.2 trillion was up 13% year on year, and client assets of $7.9 trillion were up 15% year on year, driven by continued net inflows and higher market levels. Finally, Corporate reported a net loss of $455 million, which included the net investment securities loss, as mentioned earlier, on revenue of $93 million. Turning to the outlook. I am going to update the full-year guidance by giving you the fourth quarter. Implied full-year numbers are on the page. We expect fourth-quarter NII ex-Markets to be approximately $25.5 billion and fourth-quarter total NII to be about $28 billion. And, as we have done for a couple of years, you will note we gave you a central case for 2027 NII ex-Markets of approximately $107 billion, which we will refine further next quarter. It is important to remember that this central case is based on a series of assumptions that are obviously highly uncertain, even under the best of circumstances. On expense, we expect the fourth quarter to be about $27.5 billion, with the implied full-year increase reflecting higher volume- and revenue-related expense driven by continued elevated activity levels. Finally, we continue to expect the card net charge-off rate to be approximately 3.2%. With that, we are now happy to take your questions.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: So let's open the line for Q&A. Thank you. Participants dialed in on the analyst side of today's conference call, we kindly request that you ask one question and only one related follow-up. If you would like to ask an additional question, please press. Our first question comes from Ebrahim Poonawala with Bank of America. Your line is open.

transcript.speaker: Ebrahim Poonawala
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Hey, good morning. I guess maybe one question. There has been a lot of discussion around all things AI over the last couple of months. Maybe there are two things that you can address specifically. One, when we think about the disruption risk from agentic AI, I know you have talked about this in the past. Maybe just frame that given your visibility into the technology and how you think about it. Also, the challenge of implementing agentic AI inside a bank, given the emergence of all the rogue agents: does that make it harder for a bank to actually deploy agentic AI as we think about competitive challenges?

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: I will start and then go on to the front. Yeah. Okay. So, on the disruption point, a couple of things. There has obviously been a lot of focus on Smart Cash, which I think is a small piece of the overall story. But that is live now, actually, as of the last couple of weeks. Very, very early days, and it remains a kind of targeted pilot-type thing. But it was interesting to learn some things about what clients care about and sort of see how it works to sell a product like this in the field. So, more to come on that in the future. Early days, interesting so far. I think the bigger picture here is around—you know, there have been a couple of releases of personal agents this quarter, which have really gotten a lot of attention in the market and saw a little bit of a response in bank stocks around those real developments. I guess the way we think about that from our perspective is that, on the one hand, it is nothing new, but that does not mean that we are complacent about it. So if you think about the nature of the competition that comes from these agents, it is really the intersection of two things that we have been talking about for a long time. One is yield-seeking flows. Obviously, we deal today and have dealt with all the various rate cycles and a lot of competition from yield-seeking flows. Our strategy remains focusing on primary bank share, not chasing every dollar of yield-seeking money. That does not mean that competitive pressure is not real; it just means it is not particularly new. The other piece is competition from fintechs for innovating and providing great customer experiences. We have also been talking about that for a long time, and about the criticality of ensuring that we have parity with them and that we are leading, to make sure that we are giving people the experiences they want through all the various channels, including digital. In that sense, the kind of agentic personal agents, whatever the technology is, are just the intersection of those two things, and it is not new. As I said, that does not mean we are complacent about it. We are spending a lot of time on it. It is going to be interesting to see how the space develops and what we ourselves offer there at some point. But when you take a really big step back from a competitive position, I think we really like our hand, in no small part because of the multiple decades of investment in the branch network, the value proposition, and not least the trust that our customers have in us.

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Yeah. I understand. Internally, we use agents to do things here, and we are going to continue to do that. We will use them for customers, but our focus will always be to do a great job for customers. So we are not against agents or for agents, or anything like that. They are tools. You use them for the customers. There is a defensive side, which is that you have to make sure our customers are not hurt by them. That is of concern, but think of that as an AI agenda concern, which is heightened because you do not want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them. We have always been on the side of the client. The people who are using them stand the risk. There is a liability transfer; they should not stand the liability transfer. If that is being misused, they should understand that it is being misused. So we have to make sure we protect our customer in the right kind of way. We are building tools to do that, too. In the meantime, we are not going to allow just any outside agent to come inside the company because it is just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan.

transcript.speaker: Ebrahim Poonawala
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Got it. That is good color. And just separately, as we assess the risk of interest rates maybe moving even higher than what we saw in the third quarter, what are your latest thoughts around how you assess the resiliency of the economy to handle maybe 6% on the 10-year and the Fed hiking a few times? Do you think the risk of a market event or just stress on the economy is meaningful as we discount that?

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: I think you have to—we always prepare for all different events. And that is not the same as predicting them, because we want to be a strong company, helping our clients, our communities, and countries around the world through thick or thin. So, of course, things like that could happen. I would never take it off the table. They can happen for a good reason, with a lot of demand for capital, a lot of productivity, and things being fine. They can happen for a bad reason, like sticky inflation around the world. They can happen not because of what is in the United States, but because of what happens overseas. So we are not predicting it. I have always thought there is a higher chance than other people think. I still kind of think that, but that is not a prediction. Think of that as cautious preparation.

transcript.speaker: Ebrahim Poonawala
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Got it. Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Thank you. Our next question comes from John McDonald with Truist. Your line is open.

transcript.speaker: John McDonald
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Hi, good morning, Jeremy and James. I was hoping, Jeremy, you could unpack the new outlook for 2027 NII, the central case that you gave, including some of the assumptions around balance sheet growth, deposit pricing, and the impact of higher rates?

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yeah. Sure, John. No problem. So if you start with what we have given you as the NII ex-Markets guide for the fourth quarter, which is $25.5 billion, and you annualize that, you get something like $102 billion. So we are essentially guiding to $5 billion of growth from that to the $107 billion. Of that $5 billion, probably about a quarter, I would say, is related to the yield curve. So we remain asset-sensitive and probably a little bit more asset-sensitive than the EAR shows, just because of the lower-than-modeled smart deposit betas. About a quarter of that is the hikes that are currently in the forward curve. I think there is one in December and then two through the first half of the year. The rest of it, I would actually describe pretty straightforwardly as just a continuation of the balance sheet growth and mix trends that we have seen this year. So, continued modest consumer deposit growth, continued wholesale deposit growth—probably wholesale a bit weaker than what was very strong this year, but we do not actually know—and then card loans, which obviously can be a big driver of NII, continuing at comparable levels. So actually a pretty straightforward story, I would say.

transcript.speaker: John McDonald
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Caveats, but I gave you the caveats in the prepared remarks.

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: I mean, on the one hand, I think there is more uncertainty around that number than normal because of all the things going on around the world. Obviously, it also relates to what we do, which we could change at any point in time.

transcript.speaker: John McDonald
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Okay. That is helpful. Thank you. And Jeremy, on expenses, moving over to there, do you have any preliminary thoughts on your investment spend plan for next year and the other drivers of expenses? How might those line up with the current market consensus for expenses next year?

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yeah. So we try to draw a little bit of a distinction between NII and expenses in the sense that, despite James's comments—which are obviously true—that we can modify the structure of the balance sheet to change NII, in general, undisturbed NII is a kind of property of the balance sheet at a given point in time, and it is not that sensitive to the budget cycle. Therefore, we feel like we do not have a very good excuse at this point in the year for pretending that we do not have an opinion about 2027. Expenses are a little different in the sense that they are still sensitive to the budget cycle, and there are a lot of discretionary decisions that get made in there. While we have some preliminary views, we are not done with that. You will remember, obviously, John, last year we did point out that our preliminary read on expenses suggested that the market's consensus was a bit off. That seems to be quite a bit less true this year. We see the consensus right now for 2027 expenses being around $114 billion, and our current preliminary read is not too far from that. So, kind of no news on that front, I would say. Let's see how the budget cycle finishes. As Jamie points out, I think the uncertainty is not just about the macro environment; it is also about how dynamic the investment picture is and the effects of AI, et cetera. A lot of moving parts. But for now, the consensus does not seem too far off.

transcript.speaker: John McDonald
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Okay. Got it. Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Thanks, John. Our next question comes from Erika Najarian with UBS. Your line is open.

transcript.speaker: Erika Najarian
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Yes, thank you. Good morning. My first question is just on capital management. We were fielding a lot of inbound questions from investors in terms of the $1 billion buyback versus the normal cadence of around $7 billion. I know that there is no normal cadence, and I know that buyback is the last priority. But perhaps take us through how we should think about your capital priorities, particularly given that we are hearing Basel III endgame and GSIB should be finalized at year end?

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Yeah. So I think we have told you all that we have probably $30 billion or something of excess capital, roughly, just estimating where all those endgames are, which we do not know. But that is plenty. The capital hierarchy has always been the same. After you pay your dividend, which hopefully will be steady, we really like investing in organic growth. That is the highest and best use of capital for a shareholder. Obviously, buyback comes after that, particularly when stock prices are up. The positive news is the main reason the buyback is down is that it has got nothing to do with AOCI or guessing about the environment, even Basel III. We believe now—which is different from what we told you in the past—that we can redeploy that capital at very good returns over time. Redeploying that capital at very good terms over time is far better than buying stock at a 6% or whatever the earnings yield would be if you bought it today. That is simple. That is good for shareholders. I will give you one example, and I think there are many more. The Security and Resiliency Initiative: we told you all we deployed $1.5 trillion over 10 years. I do not think we have disclosed the number, but the first year is probably over $200 billion already. We will disclose that and do some work on it, but I guess it will be considerably more than that. The world needs capital. The world needs advice. The world is becoming more complex. Assets under management around the world are bigger. So we think that is a good thing, good news in the long run. We cannot tell you what it means for the next six months, but that is why we are doing it. We hope to deploy it very well for our shareholders.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yeah. And the only thing I would add to that, Erika, is just that if you notice what the journey has been on the CET1 ratio, I want to say it started at something like 15.7%, and we are now at 13.9%. During that period, we have done a ton of internal deployment. There has been a lot of organic growth in the RWA and some of the investments that James alludes to. And during that period, we have also done a bunch of buybacks. But at this point, as Jamie says, given the speed with which we have been able to deploy organically relative to the amount of excess we have and the environment, it seems pretty clear that it makes sense to keep dry powder.

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: I am going to jump into the investment bank a little bit. They have hired a tremendous amount of very talented people in SRI, and we are lucky to have Todd and Anthony Combs here, investing some of the capital. They have had a lot of ideas. It is not just meetings at this point; they have helped fund some interesting types of things. We have more ideas. They are doing a really great policy around it, too: what can you do to accelerate security resilience in the United States around chip building? We had a big announcement in Philadelphia. I am proud of them. We have had a bunch of people who retired who raised their hands. They are coming back, more for patriotism than anything else. So it is just a great effort for the company. As we pointed out, it is global, and the global response has also been exceptional. We have something across my desk that alone is over $10 billion or $20 billion of financing in one country. So a lot more to come here. I would put in the same category the American Dream Initiative, the Innovation Economy Initiative, and the Commercial Banking initiative around the world. These things are working. We think we are doing the right kind of good business and good returns.

transcript.speaker: Erika Najarian
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: So as a follow-up here, that all sounds very positive for activity levels going forward in a very broad way. James, I know that you did some media over the past few weeks and talked about the pipeline. In that context, especially given market fears that the bond market rout around the world has a chilling effect on activity levels, maybe talk about what the pipeline looks like for activity levels in both the investment bank, both Wall Street and Main Street?

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Well, it is very good. I do think that bond volatility and market fear are not going to change what we do. We serve clients through thick or thin. We know the economic winds—I call it the weather—but that is not exactly what I am referring to. The pipeline is fine. But I have pointed out many times before that the pipeline is like an accordion. It can open and close pretty quickly. You have seen in the United States, it has been building. As Jeremy says, it was delayed. Probably—we do not really know, and we will see. I was in Europe recently, and the pipeline there is actually quite healthy, even more so in IPOs than we would have thought. So we just do not know, and serving the clients and doing a good job is the most important thing. We always forecast the pipeline, what you call the probability. And we know one thing for sure: it will be wrong.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: More to emphasize: when James and I talk about not knowing, I think we mean we do not obviously know exactly what investment banking fee revenue is going to be in the fourth quarter. I think that we do know that the overall environment is robust and supportive, and there is a lot of business that wants to get done and needs to get done. As you point out, Erika, not surprisingly, given the rate sell-off, you are going to have the market take a little bit of a breath and a pause to make sure buyers and sellers can meet on valuation terms. We did see a little bit of that slowdown in the second half of September, basically, and we will see how that plays out in the fourth quarter. But the big picture, I think, is pretty clear.

transcript.speaker: Erika Najarian
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Thank you. Our next question comes from Chris McGratty with KBW. Your line is open.

transcript.speaker: Chris McGratty
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Great, thanks. Just following up on capital allocation, maybe a comment or two on where you are less comfortable allocating capital. It seems like there are plenty of opportunities to deploy. Where are you pulling back? Where are you seeing structures or peers maybe doing something you may not want to do? Thank you.

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: I am not going to give you very specific stuff, but we are tightening up credit a little bit. I think some of the credit terms have gotten a little bit loose. You have heard us talk about that before, and other people know, too: a little too much vehicle, too-weak covenants, a little too much priming of good assets—all too much. Pushing on it, you know, we just feel you do not have to chase that kind of stuff anymore.

transcript.speaker: Chris McGratty
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Okay, great. And then secondarily, the health of the consumer is getting a lot of attention. I guess the question is durability to withstand these kinds of rates. I think you talked about 10% year-on-year spend in debit and credit. If we are a year from now and we still have rates where we are, what is your expectation for the ability for the consumer to hold on? Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: I mean, obviously, if you keep real rates very, very high for a long time, at some level that is designed to slow down economic activity to fight inflation, and it is hard to imagine that would not have an impact on the consumer. So far, what we see in the current data, and what has been true, I would say, for the last few years, is that the consumer has been quite resilient in the face of a number of headwinds that, under different circumstances, you might have expected would present a challenge. But I think the conditional expectation of consumer credit health as a function of higher rates is a fairly nuanced question. Fundamentally, the picture is pretty simple: the consumer is currently very healthy, primarily because of a healthy labor market. But if the central bank needs things to cool off and that involves an aggressive, extended rate cycle, almost by definition that is going to involve higher unemployment, which will produce weaker consumer credit results.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Thanks a lot. Our next question comes from Ken Usdin with Autonomous Research. Your line is open.

transcript.speaker: Ken Usdin
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Thanks. Hi, good morning. On the consumer side, I saw the 4% year-over-year CCB deposit growth. Just wondering, aside from agentic AI, are you seeing any change in terms of rate-seeking behavior? Is the deposit margin holding up over the last few quarters, which is also good to see? I am just wondering if there is any change in your expectations for either growth or how you are adjusting to the current marketplace and competition for deposits?

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Sure. Yeah, it is an important question. It is a good question. I think the simple answer is no significant change to our core expectations here. I think we have seen the reassertion of consumer deposit growth over the last couple of quarters as the yield-seeking flows have faded, and that continues to be our basic expectation. That is the big picture. I do think that since that outlook was shaped, we have seen a somewhat higher rate environment, and that does raise the question of what the impact of that will be on consumer deposits. In the normal course, you will obviously have higher rates paid from the high-beta products, from CDs and premium deposits. All else equal, you would probably expect some amount of additional internal migration out of checking and savings into CDs or simplicity, resulting in a higher weighted-average rate paid. Maybe you see a little bit of additional outflow pressure, which results in slightly weaker deposit growth. That is all totally speculative, and it is very much a function of which side of the argument you land on. Some people believe all the cash sorting that is going to happen has already happened, and therefore these things are relatively insensitive to slightly higher rates. I do not personally believe that. It is probably a little bit more of a continuum than that, and therefore I would expect a little bit of additional pressure. But in the end, it is a matter of degree. No one really knows. The good news, I would say, is that the core franchise performance is exceptionally strong, driven in no small part by net new checking account acquisition, which I think was around 650,000 this quarter. It has really been very, very strong, and it is proof of the value proposition, the engagement we are seeing through our marketing efforts, and the power of the brand. From a long-term perspective, that is the most important thing, and the impact of rates in the near term will just be what it is.

transcript.speaker: Ken Usdin
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Excellent. Thanks, Jeremy. One follow-up on the Markets business. Obviously, we are seeing quite a bifurcation, with continued strength in equities and, as you mentioned earlier, some tougher comps, I guess, and the impact of higher rates on FICC. Any change to just client demand for balance sheet usage? It seems kind of insatiable in the equities business. Just the state of things in the Markets business in terms of activity and your willingness to provide balance sheet, but more so the demand side, too. Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yeah. So at a high level, I think the simple answer is no real change. I like your use of insatiable. Yeah, exactly. I like your insatiable-for-capital point. That feels about right. I have not heard anything to the contrary recently, frankly. But to James's point about tightening up credit, that is a little bit of an overall point about just making sure we are really scrubbing everything. In this moment where AI is such an overwhelming theme, it is producing so much innovation, and we need to think about the different pockets. Capital is being tapped through all kinds of different mechanisms. We just need to be really, really on top of things to make sure that nothing slips through.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Does that conclude your question? Thank you. Our next question comes from Mike Mayo with Wells Fargo Securities. Your line is open.

transcript.speaker: Mike Mayo
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Hi. Can you say to what degree AI helps out JPMorgan? I saw you were ranked highly in a recent AI and bank poll. But I squint and look at the earnings release, and I am trying to find the benefits, and I am not sure I can. I think—and you can update these numbers—you spend, what, $2 billion in AI, and you have maybe $2 billion of benefits, or maybe that is stale. If you could update that and also address the risk that AI agents will take deposits out of JPMorgan. As far as that answer, maybe you can talk about the value proposition and the trust and the way you protect customers' privacy and the value they place on that.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yeah. So, Mike, let me just tidy up a couple of things. First of all, on the AI expense, you are right. I think we did say that in some media setting at some point. I think it is not exactly right, and I think we corrected it later. At the time—and I think it is a little stale at this point—the AI expense number was significantly less than that. I want to say something like $700 million annually or something like that. But more importantly, there is a lot of counting effect there, right? If you price out the amount of time we are all spending thinking about it, you should probably get a higher number, too. At this point, it is not really something that you can ring-fence very well. It is diffused inside the whole institution, and it is obviously a very, very high priority. On the question of benefits, you are right. We have quantified that in the past. I am really trying to move away from that. I think that old quantification was accurate and correct as far as it went, but it included a lot of what you might call more general AI and machine learning-type stuff that is particularly significant in consumer fraud prevention and so on. While that is relevant, I think when you and others ask about AI in the current moment, you are really asking about the impact of generative and agentic AI on productivity and the expense line across a range of places, especially software engineering, but also other places. Maybe you are asking about new, exciting revenue opportunities at the margin. That, I think, is the more relevant focus right now. I am just very reluctant to spend a lot of energy quantifying it because it winds up wasting a lot of people's time inside the institution when we actually need to get them to focus on doing things. On that point, and in terms of the visibility of the benefits, I think you are right to point out that the benefits are not observable in our current quarterly earnings. I think that is probably not that surprising because, as important and dramatic and exciting as this theme is, it takes a long time to really do things that are visible at an institution of our size. I can tell you, just anecdotally for me personally, the types of use cases and benefits that I am starting to see even in my own technology organization that supports Finance are increasingly exciting. We have done some experiments with some minor legacy tools that needed to be rewritten and tried to see if we could essentially one-shot the rewrite in a couple of weeks. It did not work perfectly, but you are starting to see some really exciting opportunities for acceleration and productivity change. How long it is going to take for that to show up, we will see. Obviously, some of those benefits are going to be offset with token costs, which is a whole other conversation. We are excited; there is a lot going on. I guess your other question was the agent question and the trust question. I think I addressed some of that earlier already. At a high level, as James pointed out, the true north here is protecting the client—and the company, obviously. We are not really focusing on agents giving customers access to money movement in their accounts. I think right now some of the services that offer that do it through credential sharing, and we have a long record of being against that way of doing things: screen scraping, et cetera. It is not secure. To the extent that we are able to block those, we are blocking them to protect customers and protect ourselves. It is important that customers understand that if they give up their credentials to the agent and the agent does something they do not want, that is going to be on them. That is not an ideal state of things. We are working on being able to do this correctly. That is a piece of the puzzle. In the big picture, trust is clearly an asset, and we have spent decades building it. As I said previously, we like our hand in that respect. But we need to be clear that the fact that we are trusted is not an excuse for complacency or a reason to provide a mediocre customer experience. We really need to do both at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Mike Mayo
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: And one short follow-up on the token costs. Do you get a benefit from scale with the token cost, say, versus a small bank? And are you also transitioning more toward open-model AI systems that can cost a lot less?

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: It is a little bit of everything. I would say our strategy is quite focused on minimizing lock-in and maximizing optionality and the ability to manage costs. Part of the strategy is model agnosticism, harness agnosticism, and the ability to run both proprietary models and open-weight and open-source models, some of which we have run on our own. It is very much an all-of-the-above strategy designed to get the best of what is available at the best price and control our own investment.

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: And there are tools coming for model routing, which send it to the best, quickest, cheapest model. We do not need the most expensive thing for every query you have, and very often people just use the one they are comfortable with. So that is all coming, to have that, of course, under control.

transcript.speaker: Mike Mayo
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Great. All right. Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Thanks, Mike. Our next question comes from Gerard Cassidy with RBC. Your line is open.

transcript.speaker: Gerard Cassidy
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Hi, Jeremy. Hi, James. Can you share with us the deposit beta outlook? Obviously, interest rates are starting to go up. Fed funds futures are suggesting more rate increases over the next three to six months. With your growth in your consumer deposit base since the last tightening cycle in 2022 and 2023, how are you thinking about what you might see this time around? Also, obviously, we are starting from a much higher interest rate level than we did in 2022. Could that mean deposit betas may not be as high this time around for you folks?

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: So it is a very good question, Gerard, and I think it is an important thing for people to be thinking about because this particular rate cycle, this latest rate cycle, is arguably even more unprecedented than the last one. We just do not have a lot of historical data about how people behave when you see rate hikes from the launch point that we have seen this cycle. It has been an unusual 10-plus years, I would say, and I think it is quite important for people to realize, especially people who are doing this by training models on historical data, that the historical data set is just not that rich. So it is very important to be thinking out of the box. In that context, though, I think locally our beta story is pretty easy, actually, in the sense that you can almost think about the franchise as pretty barbelled between a bunch of very high-beta deposits, like most of wholesale, as well as CDs and premium deposits and consumer, and then a stack of very low-beta deposits. The question is probably less the pricing of any given product, although that has always been a response to competition and market conditions, and more a sort of migration behavior across products in this cycle. I do not think we have—our local expectations are that it is going to behave roughly the way it has been behaving. But I do think it is right to note that this is a different cycle, and therefore we have to be thinking about all scenarios, as we always do.

transcript.speaker: Gerard Cassidy
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Very good. And then pivoting over to a different question, the IMF came out very recently this month with the global stability report. They have talked about how the hedge fund industry has grown dramatically and is now, in their eyes, a systemic risk. Leveraged finance in particular was highlighted as another high risk. Obviously, that is in your wheelhouse, as it is with your peers and competitors. Can you share with us your insights on how you are managing these risks and what you worry about, since these businesses are now so much bigger today than they were 10 or 15 years ago?

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: We could say we worry about a lot of stuff. I do not know what the IMF thinks about it.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: But they are not wrong, because there is a lot of leverage in some of this stuff. It is not wrong, but it is also a little bit obvious. I would also say it is not really new. The hedge fund industry has been relevant to our franchise for decades now, and a source of risk for the system for a long time. Everyone knows that, including the hedge funds themselves, which are increasingly institutionalized, with very professional risk management and control over their margin relationships and so on. There is risk; obviously, that is the business. It is about knowing it, managing it, and preparing for the unknown. I would say hedge fund leverage as a contributor of risk to the system is very much in the category of known unknowns. It does not mean it is riskless, but we kind of know what it is.

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: There are a couple of unwinds that happened recently, not huge, some on the equity side and some on the fixed-income arbitrage side, and they were handled pretty easily by the Street.

transcript.speaker: Gerard Cassidy
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Very good. Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Thank you. Our next question comes from Glenn Schorr with Evercore ISI. Your line is open.

transcript.speaker: Glenn Schorr
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Hi. One quick follow-up on the whole agentic and AI impact across the portfolio. My question is your comfort level and ability to protect from the standpoint of how you and the regulators are thinking about liquidity stress testing and liquidity risk management. Just by the nature of the technology existing, do things change? I do not know if I am getting too far into the future here, but, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: No, I understand the question. You can argue that it is sort of downstream of the narrative that the SVB run was a social media phenomenon. We were never big buyers of that idea. I think the better way to understand that situation was as an extremely concentrated and undiversified deposit base that was wholesale, non-operational, and kind of monoculture in terms of who was shaping the thinking around that. Arguably, in a world with TV and fax machines, I think you probably would have gotten essentially the same answer in terms of the speed of the run. The processing of the fax machines into wires might have taken an additional eight hours, but the core ingredients were the same. Everyone is pretty eager to tell a fast-deposit-run story in this new technology-enabled world. I am just a little bit less persuaded that you really have those effects. In a world with agentic consumer cash movement, it is easy to create a story where it becomes even easier to move cash under certain types of crises. But I think the right way to ensure that your deposits are stable is to run the company with fortress principles so that people are confident in you. You are probably not supposed to be hoping that your deposits are stable because the money is difficult to move. That is what I would say.

transcript.speaker: Glenn Schorr
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: I think that is fair. I appreciate that.

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: If you take a big step further, we have $1.5 trillion of cash and marketable securities, so we are not worried about changing our liquidity. But take a big step back: banking services are necessary—credit cards and debit cards and money and insured deposits, and you need the branches. One of the ways you earn that is NII from money that sits idle. But if you could not do it that way, over time you would do something different: subscription, of course, or investment accounts combined with checking accounts. Over time, it will adjust. We want to do a great job for our clients. It will cost a lot of money to run these banking systems; most of it is a fixed cost. We are not worried about that over time. But in the short run, of course, you have to figure out how you want to handle that kind of stuff. I do think you raise a different issue, which is: should regulators be thinking about what they are going to do with some of these things? Yeah, of course they should. It is a new world, and with all these bots and agents and stuff like that, could someone get hurt and cause a problem? Maybe. I would already try to be prepared for that.

transcript.speaker: Glenn Schorr
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: One question on concentration risk. The public equity markets do not know anything about that and do not care, but bank loan books and bond books and insurance portfolios do. My question is: with this amazing hyperscaler race to expand compute power, and everybody wanting to finance it, the money and capital are there, but from your vantage point, can we finance it without breaking some concentration limits? Can the market digest what the capex numbers suggest for the spend?

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yeah, it is a really good question, right? We think a lot about our current exposure to that. Arguably, the more important question is our appetite for future exposure in light of the announced amount of capex that needs to happen in this ecosystem and the associated demands or requirements for capital from the financial system. A couple of things: clearly, single-issuer concentration is the thing that is going to get managed. Given the nature of these structures, you have to be sophisticated about assessing both your indirect exposure and your direct exposure, where you sit on the capital structure, and the value of the collateral. There is a lot of nuanced credit analysis that needs to be done correctly to assess your individual issuer exposure across the ecosystem. You can assume that institutions are going to contain that. One thing we have seen over the last year is increasing usage of different parts of the capital markets ecosystem to get as much diversified financing of this build-out as possible. There is a lot of capital out there waiting to be deployed, so some of it will be from the banking system and some of it will be from elsewhere. At the system level, I do not know; some people are talking about crowding-out effects, so that will be interesting to see. For us, we need to focus on our institutional risk appetite. In addition to the obvious single-name focus, the other thing to be very careful about is just the AI theme, because the AI theme is so broadly diffused into the marketplace. It is not just traditional construction lending. Now increasingly, it is working-capital revolvers. You also get the equity markets. It is kind of everywhere. You really need to be running stresses that test your resilience to a meaningful change in overall thinking across the entire enterprise. That is something that we spend a lot of time thinking about. Currently, our exposures are still quite modest in the context of our overall wholesale exposure, but that is not the same as saying that we would be immune to a major change in sentiment in the AI space. I think I would be surprised if anyone, frankly, was immune to that at this point.

transcript.speaker: Glenn Schorr
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: That is great. Thanks so much, Jeremy.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Thanks, Glenn. Next, we will go to the line of Manan Gosalia from Morgan Stanley. Your line is open.

transcript.speaker: Manan Gosalia
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: I wanted to check in on the commercial banking side. What are you seeing with your core middle-market client? Is there an insatiable demand for capital there, too? Or, as short-end rates move higher and the value of the curve moves higher, are you seeing any pullback in demand there?

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yes. I do not think that when we talk about the insatiable demand for capital, we are talking about our core middle-market clients. I think their theme for some time now has been people worrying about other people while doing fine themselves. The theme is always, oh, we run these surveys, and they are always, I am worried about this, I am worried about that. And then, how are you doing? Oh, I am doing great. So it is kind of an interesting dynamic there. No question that higher rates, input costs, inflation, the diesel narrative—these things are tough for middle-market clients, and so we see them trying to manage that to the best of their ability. I think it does create a little bit of caution in that space. But I think balance sheets are strong. People have been through a lot over the last few years, so they are well prepared. I do not think insatiable demand for capital applies to that subset of the client base.

transcript.speaker: Manan Gosalia
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Got it. And then separately, Jeremy, on the liquidity side, in the past you have noted that you need to see changes in liquidity rules to fully realize the impact of freeing up excess capital. As we get closer to the regulators coming out with new liquidity proposals, and if you do get more credit for discount-window readiness, how would that change how you manage the balance sheet, and over what time frame?

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: I just know—I think it is right for the regulators to look at all these things again. It is not just the discount window; it is FHLB, inconsistencies between resolution and recovery, what counts as HQLA to start with, and how you do LCR. I think they should look at all that, with the view that you can create safer banks with more deployed capital and more liquidity if you use intermediate markets, and that should be the goal. But it is really hard to answer the question because this is going to be up to them. Either way, we will serve our clients, do a good job, take care of them, and do what we are supposed to do. I think they should be doing that, so we will see. We do not have to speculate about what they are going to do. There are a lot of proposals out there that are part of international rules. I applaud them for looking at it.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yeah. I agree with everything James said, and it is particularly complicated across a range of dimensions. I will note that at Company Update, we actually talked about this and in some sense gave you the answer. What we said at the time was that the problem with the situation where the system has a healthy amount of capital that is relatively constrained is that, just at the margin, it leads you to have your asset deployment be in much higher risk-density instruments, essentially. A place where you are a little bit more balanced would tend to move you towards lower risk density, and it just enables you to serve a broader part of the economy, including mortgages, consumer lending, and also some of the more secured C&I-type structures.

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Yeah. If they want to reduce the size of the Fed balance sheet, they are going to make some changes.

transcript.speaker: Manan Gosalia
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Got it. Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Our next question comes from Matt O'Connor with Deutsche Bank.

transcript.speaker: Matt O'Connor
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Good morning. I was hoping you could talk more about how you are growing noninterest-bearing deposits when a number of peers are not. And then, just how you are thinking about that specific bucket of deposits in a higher-rate environment: can you continue to grow them?

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yes. I think I have addressed that point to some degree in connection with my answer to John's question on the 2027 NII outlook and how we are feeling about consumer deposit growth. But just to reiterate a couple of points: number one, our net new checking account growth has been exceptionally strong, 650,000 this quarter. People are reacting; they are responding well to the marketing, the brand, the value proposition, and the multi-decade investment in the product bundle that we offer our consumers. I think that is really good news and has been a contributor to the reassertion of consumer deposit growth. As I noted, the question a little bit in this rate-hiking cycle is going to be how those balances behave, how pricing pressure behaves, how much migration we see to higher-beta products, and so on. We will see. I think we are relatively optimistic right now, and we would not expect radical changes for small local moves. But we do think a lot about the different rate regimes and how they can affect deposit beta. I think that is part of just being prepared for everything.

transcript.speaker: Matt O'Connor
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Okay. And I guess I was thinking more specifically about noninterest-bearing deposits, which I think are more on the commercial corporate side of things. I was just trying to see if there is any color there in terms of cash management products, things that have been a key driver.

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Most of the noninterest-bearing deposits are consumer, and that is because we are growing the business. There are different products for different types of consumers. I think the wholesale side, the commercial side, is much more competitive than that.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yeah. No, I think, to be honest, the reporting is a little confusing, in part because of the famous ECR product that sometimes makes it look like on the wholesale side there are more noninterest-bearing deposits than there actually are. That is just an artifact of the rules for how we have to report. If you want to get more color on that, Matt, you can with the IR team. At a high level, I would say that wholesale deposits have been, continue to be, and at the margin are a little bit more competitive. But the way to think about that is not that the product offering allows us to grow noninterest-bearing deposits. There is an overall margin that you earn on your deposits as part of the bundle of products, and that is a function of how good your service offering is. We have quite a good track record there of winning share and winning mandates. It is a function of the quality of our products.

transcript.speaker: Matt O'Connor
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Okay. Understood. Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Thanks, Matt. Our next question comes from David Chiaverini with Jefferies. Your line is open.

transcript.speaker: David Chiaverini
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Hi, thanks for taking the question. JPMorgan's ROTCE target through the cycle is 17% versus 21% today. Is there anything you are seeing either in the macro environment or the competitive environment that could accelerate a path to 17%, or is that not anywhere on the horizon?

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: I have always talked about the 17% being through the cycle. Things are pretty good now, with high volume, high asset prices, and fairly low credit losses and all that. If you could earn 17% consistently for a long period of time, that is a really good return for shareholders. That is our goal. I do not want to change every time something happens in the marketplace.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: So far, so good, and we will go. Hopefully, we will enjoy this good environment for a while. We do not know when it is going to stop.

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: And we do not want to be pointlessly negative, and I will not bore you with the speech. But if you just look across the entire franchise, every single business is performing exceptionally well.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: The conditions have just been exceptionally favorable.

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Every company.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yeah. It is not just us. That has not historically been true. Historically, you have tended to see a bit more internal diversification, with high-rate environments making some businesses do better than others and vice versa. The conditions we have had recently, where essentially every part of the franchise is beating records, are not typical by historical standards.

transcript.speaker: David Chiaverini
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Makes sense. Thanks for that. And then, shifting to credit quality on the consumer side, could you talk about corporate credit health? It looks like you have built some reserves on the wholesale side. Curious about your comments there.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Sure. Yeah, the wholesale build is actually just from new activity. So it is not downgrades or a change in the outlook or anything like that. I would say that the corporate credit outlook is currently pretty stable. But obviously, there are issues out there, and we will have to see how those flow through. The performance of our borrowers, energy prices, fuel inputs, and higher rates are all things that will create challenges in different pockets of the economy and the C&I space, as well as the CRE space, for that matter. We will see. So far, it is very early, but in general we think corporate balance sheets are in quite good shape, and there has been resilience. But there are a lot of pressures building up, so we will have to see what happens.

transcript.speaker: David Chiaverini
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Great. Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Thank you. Our final question comes from Kunpeng Ma from China Securities. Your line is open.

transcript.speaker: Kunpeng Ma
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Hi, good morning. Good morning, James and Jeremy. This is from China Securities. I have a question on the revenue of the Markets business. We have seen some volatility in market revenue across quarters, so I do not know whether we have a meaningful estimate of the flow-through of quarterly Markets business revenue. Also, if you can provide us with some of your thoughts on the key business momentum supporting such an estimate, that would be very helpful. Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Jeremy Barnum
transcript.title: CFO
transcript.content: Yeah. So I had trouble exactly following your question, but I think you are asking me for a fourth-quarter outlook for Markets revenue. As you know, we do not actually guide to that. It is obviously very, very hard to predict and essentially a function of outside forces. Just a reminder that you do tend to see significant seasonal decline between the third and the fourth quarter. Also a reminder that in recent years we have had some slightly unusual seasonal patterns between the third and fourth quarter. Our base-case assumptions right now, all else being equal, are normal seasonal declines between the third and fourth quarter. Make sure that you interpret normal with the right amount of historical context. All the usual caveats apply. We have seen a lot of volatility; there is a lot going on, and anything can happen.

transcript.speaker: James Dimon
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: I think the fourth quarter will not have the same seasonal decline. First, there is too much going on in the world.

transcript.speaker: Kunpeng Ma
transcript.title: Analyst
transcript.content: Thank you. Thank you so much.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Thanks very much. That is all the time we have for questions today. Thank you very much, everybody. Thank you all for participating in today's conference. You may disconnect at this time, and have a great rest of your day.
